newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire tightens emergency rule over troubled east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire tightens emergency rule over troubled east.

text.p: Zaire has banned public meetings in its two troubled eastern provinces and suspended commercial air links as part of emergency measures to contain ethnic warfare.
A government spokesman said on Monday night that the measures followed a weekend declaration of a state of emergency in North and South Kivu, which have been placed under military rule.
"The government has decided to restrict public and individual liberties in these two provinces," spokesman Boguo Makeli told state radio. "It concerns the movement of people."
He said the emergency rule order was given by President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has been in a Swiss clinic since his prostate cancer operation on August 22.
Fighting between the Zairean army and ethnic Tutsi rebels has pushed the vast Central African nation of 45 million people to the brink of disintegration, diplomats say.
The prospect of a breakup has increased with the absence of Mobutu, who has held the chaotic country together during more than 30 years of strongman rule.

Aid workers say about half a million displaced people are roaming the bush in search of safe havens, and the conflict threatens to draw in the Tutsi-dominated armies of neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.
"The government has decided to reinforce its military and civilian intelligence operation in the east. More members of SNIP (military intelligence) will be brought in," Boguo said.
He said about half a million Rwandan refugees still in camp in eastern Zaire were banned from leaving their shelters. "Those contravening the order would be expelled."
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo followed the emergency rule order with the appointment of military governors -- General Ngala Panzu for North Kivu and General Elesse Yombentole for South Kivu.
Ngala Panzu commanded a military crackdown earlier this year against ethnic Tutsis in the Masisi region east of the North Kivu capital Goma.

Kengo accuses Rwanda and Burundi of backing the Banyamulenge Tutsis who settled in Zaire from Rwanda at the end of the 18th Century. State television at the weekend paraded 10 people it said were Rwandan prisoners of war captured trying to blow up the airport in the South Kivu capital Bukavu.
Rwanda and Burundi deny any involvement and accuse Zaire of trying to expel the 300,000 Banyamulenge instead of recognising them as Zairean.
Kengo said on Monday he was confident the situation in the east would be brought under control.
"With the appointment of new military authorities, Zaire will overcome this crisis," he said after meeting the Congolese prime minister. "Today the situation is much better than it was yesterday."
Zaire's transitional parliament scheduled a special session on Tuesday to approve the emergency rule order.
